concepts.title: Three different limits
concepts.explain: Aircraft weight, center of gravity (CG), and lateral balance each influence how safely an airplane can fly. Meeting one limit does not excuse missing another.
concepts.apply: Before takeoff, confirm both loaded weight and CG are approved.

concepts.title: Too much weight
concepts.explain: Excess weight typically lengthens takeoff roll, reduces climb rate, increases stall speed and stresses aircraft structure.
concepts.apply: A long runway does not make an overweight airplane legal or safe.

concepts.title: Forward center of gravity
concepts.explain: A CG too far forward generally demands greater tail-down force and elevator authority; it can make rotation or flare difficult.
concepts.apply: Heavy baggage in the nose or a forward-heavy loading pattern can create a control problem.

concepts.title: Aft center of gravity
concepts.explain: As CG moves aft, longitudinal stability usually decreases; stall or spin recovery may become more difficult, even if elevator forces feel lighter.
concepts.apply: An aft-limit exceedance is not a harmless way to improve performance.

concepts.title: Lateral balance
concepts.explain: Uneven fuel or loading can make one wing heavy. Holding constant corrective aileron increases drag and workload.
concepts.apply: Use appropriate fuel management and consider lateral loading where relevant.

check.question: An aircraft is below maximum gross weight but outside the aft CG limit. Can you depart?
options: No; weight and CG both must meet approved limits
check.explanation: Approved CG limits apply independently of the maximum weight limit.

concepts.title: Lift must support weight
concepts.explain: In steady, unaccelerated level flight, lift balances weight. Heavier aircraft need more lift to maintain that condition.
concepts.apply: A heavier aircraft may need greater angle of attack or airspeed.

concepts.title: Weight increases stall speed
concepts.explain: More weight requires additional lift; because maximum lift coefficient is limited, stall speed increases at higher weight.
concepts.apply: Never assume the same margin above stall speed at every loading.

concepts.title: Weight hurts climb
concepts.explain: More weight generally increases the power required, reducing excess power and climb performance.
concepts.apply: A high-altitude or hot-day departure can compound the problem.

concepts.title: Weight affects landing
concepts.explain: Higher landing weight normally raises approach and touchdown speeds and increases landing distance.
concepts.apply: Do not use a light-weight landing estimate for a heavy arrival.

concepts.title: Do not confuse weight with balance
concepts.explain: Removing cargo may solve excess weight but could shift CG outside the envelope if removed from the wrong station.
concepts.apply: Recompute the full condition after changing the load.

check.question: Which change usually makes a takeoff more demanding?
options: A weight change never affects performance
check.explanation: Heavier loading typically increases takeoff distance and degrades climb performance.

concepts.title: What center of gravity means
concepts.explain: CG is the point where the airplane’s weight is considered concentrated for balance calculations. Its location changes as people, bags, and fuel are moved or consumed.
concepts.apply: The airplane can start and end a flight at different CG locations.

concepts.title: CG versus center of lift
concepts.explain: The relationship between aerodynamic forces and CG determines pitching moments. Airplanes are designed around specified loading ranges.
concepts.apply: Do not infer safe handling from how the airplane sits on the ramp.

concepts.title: Forward CG handling
concepts.explain: Forward loading tends to increase longitudinal stability but can limit nose-up authority for takeoff rotation or landing flare.
concepts.apply: The most stable feeling is not automatically the safest loading.

concepts.title: Aft CG handling
concepts.explain: Aft loading reduces longitudinal stability and can reduce stall and spin recovery margins.
concepts.apply: Respect the aft limit even when control forces seem manageable.

concepts.title: Fuel burn moves CG
concepts.explain: Fuel tanks have arms. As fuel is consumed, total weight and the moment change; CG can move forward or aft.
concepts.apply: Check any required takeoff and landing CG conditions.

check.question: Why might an airplane become harder to recover from a stall with an aft CG?
options: Aft CG can reduce stability and nose-down recovery authority
check.explanation: Aft loading can reduce longitudinal stability and stall recovery capability.

concepts.title: Where the limits come from
concepts.explain: The approved aircraft flight manual, weight-and-balance records, type certificate data and applicable supplements establish the relevant aircraft-specific limits.
concepts.apply: Use the actual airplane and configuration, not figures from a similar model.

concepts.title: Basic empty weight changes
concepts.explain: Equipment installation, paint, alterations and repairs can change empty weight and CG. Current records matter.
concepts.apply: Verify the updated empty-weight entry after modifications.

concepts.title: Aircraft loading is a legal limit
concepts.explain: Operating limitations under 14 CFR 91.9 and the approved aircraft information govern the flight.
concepts.apply: A valid pilot certificate does not authorize flight outside aircraft limits.

concepts.title: Useful preflight inputs
concepts.explain: Gather aircraft empty weight and moment/CG, passenger and baggage weights and locations, usable fuel and planned fuel burn.
concepts.apply: A spreadsheet is only as reliable as the inputs.

concepts.title: Know the unit system
concepts.explain: Many FAA examples use pounds, inches and inch-pounds. Manufacturers may use index values or different reference datums.
concepts.apply: Do not mix kilograms, pounds or arm systems without a deliberate conversion.

check.question: You find an old loading sheet but the avionics were replaced. What should you do?
options: Confirm current equipment and updated weight-and-balance records
check.explanation: A modification can change the aircraft’s approved empty weight and moment.

concepts.title: Reference datum
concepts.explain: A manufacturer-selected imaginary vertical plane from which longitudinal distances are measured. The datum location can differ between airplane models.
concepts.apply: Always use the datum defined for the airplane.

concepts.title: Station
concepts.explain: A station is an identified location measured relative to the datum. Seating, fuel tanks and baggage areas have station information.
concepts.apply: Select the correct station for each load.

concepts.title: Arm
concepts.explain: Arm is the signed distance from the reference datum to the item’s CG. Arms aft of the datum are generally positive under a common convention, but check the specific aircraft system.
concepts.apply: Never silently change signs or reference points.

concepts.title: CG range
concepts.explain: The approved CG range is the allowed fore-and-aft interval, often varying by gross weight.
concepts.apply: A fixed single CG number is not enough to describe every limit.

concepts.title: Loading envelope
concepts.explain: The envelope graphs allowed combinations of loaded weight and CG or moment; inside the approved outline is required.
concepts.apply: A plotted point just outside the outline is not acceptable.

check.question: What determines the numerical arm of an installed item?
options: Its distance from the manufacturer’s reference datum
check.explanation: An arm is a distance from the aircraft-specific reference datum.

concepts.title: Core equation
concepts.explain: Moment = weight × arm. In conventional U.S. examples, pounds multiplied by inches gives pound-inches (lb-in).
concepts.apply: Write down units when building your calculation.

concepts.title: Simple worked example
concepts.explain: A 40 lb bag at an arm of 95 inches contributes 3,800 lb-in of moment (40 × 95).
concepts.apply: A bag can be relatively light yet influential if far from the datum.

concepts.title: Two similar weights
concepts.explain: A 50 lb load at 100 inches creates 5,000 lb-in, while 50 lb at 50 inches creates 2,500 lb-in. The farther load has twice the moment.
concepts.apply: Distance matters as much as weight for CG effect.

concepts.title: Balance analogy
concepts.explain: A seesaw balances when opposing moments are equal—not necessarily when weights on both sides are equal.
concepts.apply: Use moment relationships rather than guessing by weight alone.

concepts.title: Manufacturer moment indexes
concepts.explain: Some charts print moments divided by 100 or 1,000 to keep tables readable. Apply the stated index scale consistently.
concepts.apply: A moment scale error can place your CG in the wrong spot.

check.question: A 30 lb bag is located at an arm of 120 in. What is its moment?

concepts.title: Build a loading table
concepts.explain: Record every item as weight, arm and moment. Include current basic empty aircraft data, occupants, baggage and fuel according to the approved method.
concepts.apply: Do not substitute maximum seat capacity for the actual occupants.

concepts.title: Sum all weights
concepts.explain: Total weight is the sum of all load weights including the airplane itself. Use fuel weight based on the correct fuel type and amount.
concepts.apply: Confirm the total is below applicable structural and phase-of-flight limits.

concepts.title: Sum all moments
concepts.explain: Total moment is the sum of each weight × arm, using the proper signs and any published index convention.
concepts.apply: Incorrect arm data can matter more than arithmetic precision.

concepts.title: Find loaded CG
concepts.explain: Loaded CG arm = total moment ÷ total weight. Example: 180,000 lb-in ÷ 2,400 lb = 75 in.
concepts.apply: Compare that position with the approved limits for this gross weight.

concepts.title: Worked data are illustrations
concepts.explain: The handbook’s example aircraft and loading tables teach method; they are not safe limits for your trainer.
concepts.apply: Look up your airplane’s current weight-and-balance report.

check.question: A 2,000 lb aircraft load has a moment of 160,000 lb-in. The CG arm is…
check.explanation: Divide total moment 160,000 by total weight 2,000 to get 80 inches.

concepts.title: Start with the correct chart
concepts.explain: A loading graph converts weight at a particular station into moment or a moment index. Each airplane’s published graph is different.
concepts.apply: Check its axis labels and scale before reading values.

concepts.title: Select weight for the station
concepts.explain: Locate the known weight on the relevant chart axis, trace across or upward as instructed, and intersect the correct load-line or arm.
concepts.apply: Using a passenger line for baggage creates a plausible but wrong moment.

concepts.title: Read the moment carefully
concepts.explain: Follow the chart’s grid in the correct direction and note whether moments are divided by 100 or 1,000.
concepts.apply: Record the scale explicitly in your worksheet.

concepts.title: Add all loaded moments
concepts.explain: Combine basic empty aircraft and each occupant, baggage and fuel contribution to compute the total loaded moment.
concepts.apply: Check arithmetic before you interpret the envelope.

concepts.title: Use the table method as a cross-check
concepts.explain: If you have weights and arms, multiplying weight by arm can validate a chart value.
concepts.apply: A major disagreement suggests a misread axis or wrong index.

check.question: What is a major risk when using the moment-loading graph?
options: Using the wrong station line or index scale
Checking the chart against the POH
check.explanation: Incorrect station lines and moment scales can yield a dangerously wrong CG.

title: Plot weight and CG in the envelope

concepts.title: What an envelope represents
concepts.explain: An approved envelope shows the permissible weight versus CG or total moment combinations. The shape may narrow at lower weights.
concepts.apply: Do not test only the maximum weight line.

concepts.title: Identify the axes
concepts.explain: Some graphs use CG in inches; others use total moment or a scaled moment index. Read the printed labels.
concepts.apply: Do not put a calculated CG in inches on a total-moment axis.

concepts.title: Plot the loaded point
concepts.explain: Trace the actual calculated gross weight to the actual CG/moment value. The intersection must fall inside the permitted region.
concepts.apply: A point outside either edge is a no-go until loading changes.

concepts.title: Check additional limitations
concepts.explain: Maximum ramp, takeoff and landing weights may be distinct; usable fuel and special loadings can add restrictions.
concepts.apply: Consider loading as it changes during taxi and flight.

concepts.title: Use the published chart
concepts.explain: A screenshot, generic calculator or conceptual diagram never overrides the current approved chart for the aircraft.
concepts.apply: Recalculate if passengers or baggage change before departure.

check.question: A plotted point is below maximum gross weight but outside the forward CG boundary. Is it acceptable?
options: Yes, if weight is below maximum
No; it must also be within the CG envelope
check.explanation: Both the applicable weight and CG boundaries must be satisfied.

concepts.title: Fuel is movable weight
concepts.explain: Fuel contributes both weight and moment. Its effect depends on the tank’s approved station arm.
concepts.apply: Use correct usable fuel and fuel weight for the aircraft and fuel type.

concepts.title: Takeoff loading
concepts.explain: Calculate the anticipated weight and balance at the appropriate pre-takeoff condition.
concepts.apply: Do not ignore fuel added after the initial calculation.

concepts.title: Landing loading
concepts.explain: Subtract expected fuel burn weight and corresponding fuel moment to recompute the arrival condition when required.
concepts.apply: An initially legal CG can shift as fuel burns.

concepts.title: Different tanks can matter
concepts.explain: Fuel in wing, auxiliary or tip tanks may have different longitudinal/lateral effects.
concepts.apply: Use the AFM/POH fuel-management procedures and limitations.

concepts.title: Worst-case load states
concepts.explain: For loading close to a boundary, assess relevant portions of the trip rather than assuming one calculation covers the entire flight.
concepts.apply: Recheck after changes in planned fuel use or passenger loading.

check.question: Why calculate CG again after expected fuel burn?
options: CG can shift as fuel weight and moment decrease
Fuel has weight but no moment
check.explanation: Fuel’s moment is removed along with its weight, so the total CG can move.

title: Variable station arms and load plans

concepts.title: Some loads have variable arms
concepts.explain: Long baggage areas and certain seating or cargo stations may use ranges rather than a single arm. Use the prescribed assumptions.
concepts.apply: Avoid guessing a center point for unusually positioned cargo.

concepts.title: Loading schedule placards
concepts.explain: Published loading diagrams may identify seating stations, baggage areas and fuel locations.
concepts.apply: Use the station designations exactly as labeled.

concepts.title: Unusual airplane layouts
concepts.explain: Multiseat aircraft can have multiple cabin rows, forward and aft baggage compartments and different fuel tanks.
concepts.apply: More cabin space creates more possible out-of-envelope combinations.

concepts.title: Model-specific conventions
concepts.explain: Some tables use negative arms or manufacturer-defined datum locations.
concepts.apply: Follow the specific sign conventions and graph scales in your AFM.

concepts.title: Record the final plan
concepts.explain: Record measured or reasonable actual load weights and recalculate after major changes.
concepts.apply: A neat table does not substitute for correct source inputs.

check.question: What should you do when your airplane’s moment chart uses a different scale than the sample?
options: Follow the scale printed on your own aircraft chart
check.explanation: The correct approved graph and moment/index convention are aircraft-specific.

concepts.title: Moving a load changes moment
concepts.explain: When an existing load moves within the airplane, total weight stays constant but its moment changes.
concepts.apply: You can adjust CG without changing gross weight, but only within loading limits.

concepts.title: Moment change equation
concepts.explain: Change in moment = weight moved × distance moved, using signs for direction.
concepts.apply: An aft move increases aft moment in the common positive-aft convention.

concepts.title: CG change equation
concepts.explain: CG shift = (weight moved × distance moved) ÷ total aircraft weight.
concepts.apply: Ensure the total weight uses the same units.

concepts.title: Worked shift example
concepts.explain: Moving a 40 lb bag 30 inches aft in a 2,400 lb airplane shifts the CG aft by (40 × 30)/2,400 = 0.5 inch.
concepts.apply: Half an inch can matter near an envelope boundary.

concepts.title: Adding or removing load differs
concepts.explain: If weight is added or removed, both total weight and total moment change; recompute CG from new totals.
concepts.apply: Do not use the shifting-only equation for an added passenger.

check.question: A 50 lb bag moves 20 in aft inside a 2,000 lb airplane. Approximate CG shift?

concepts.title: First find the constraint
concepts.explain: Determine whether the issue is gross weight, forward CG or aft CG. Different problems require different remedies.
concepts.apply: Removing any random item can worsen the CG.

concepts.title: Reduce excess gross weight
concepts.explain: An overweight airplane needs legal weight reduction; moving weight inside the airplane cannot solve maximum gross weight exceedance.
concepts.apply: Reduce loading without compromising fuel reserve or other safety requirements.

concepts.title: Correct forward CG
concepts.explain: Subject to aircraft procedures and capacity, shift permissible weight aft or change loading to move the CG aft.
concepts.apply: Recompute the complete table and check limits.

concepts.title: Correct aft CG
concepts.explain: Subject to load limits, move permissible weight forward or otherwise adjust loading until the computed position is approved.
concepts.apply: Avoid assuming that a small shift is sufficient.

concepts.title: Check every compartment and floor limit
concepts.explain: Even when aircraft gross weight and CG are legal, station or baggage compartment limits can still prohibit the load.
concepts.apply: Read the placard and POH limits for each station.

check.question: An aircraft exceeds maximum gross weight but its CG is centered. Will moving bags solve the excess weight?
options: Yes, moving bags changes gross weight
check.explanation: Changing where weight sits cannot decrease total aircraft weight.

concepts.title: Step 1: identify the airplane
concepts.explain: Locate its current empty weight, empty CG/moment and the correct approved manual and loading sheets.
concepts.apply: Aircraft revisions and equipment matter.

concepts.title: Step 2: gather accurate loads
concepts.explain: Include actual occupants, baggage, usable fuel and other items with the correct station arms.
concepts.apply: Ask for realistic weights; do not assume identical occupants.

concepts.title: Step 3: compute
concepts.explain: Sum weights and moments and derive CG. Use the proper chart scale for that aircraft.
concepts.apply: Double-check signs, units and math.

concepts.title: Step 4: compare
concepts.explain: Confirm applicable takeoff and landing weights, CG envelope, station limits and fuel movement effects.
concepts.apply: All conditions must be satisfied—not merely one.

concepts.title: Step 5: make the safe decision
concepts.explain: If load is out of limits or data are missing, delay, unload, redistribute lawfully or seek qualified guidance before flight.
concepts.apply: Airworthiness begins before starting the engine.

check.question: Passenger baggage changes after you finish your weight-and-balance worksheet. What now?
options: Update the load calculation and verify all limits again
check.explanation: Any changed load can change aircraft weight and CG; recompute before relying on the result.
